title: Which has more?
keyIdea: To compare two groups, look, match or count. With 1, 2 or 3 things you can often just see which group has more. To match, pair each thing in one group with a thing in the other: the group with things left over has more, and if nothing is left over they are the same. Counting works too: the bigger number is more. Spreading things out or squashing them up does not change how many there are, and big things are not more than small things unless there are more of them. Fewer means not as many.

kid: Look at two plates. One has 2 grapes. One has 4. The plate with 4 has more. The plate with 2 has fewer.
Not sure? Match them up. Put one of your cars next to one of mine. Do it again and again. If I have a car with no partner, I have more.
A long row is not always more. Spread out 4 cars and they make a long line. Squash up 5 cars and the line is short. But 5 is still more than 4.
Big things are not always more. 3 big balls and 5 tiny beads: count them. 5 is more than 3, so the beads win.
adult: This is early number: comparing quantities. Development Matters asks three and four year olds to compare quantities using words like more than and fewer than. By the end of Reception the Early Learning Goal is to compare quantities up to 10 and say when one is greater than, less than or the same as the other.

Children use three ways to compare. Subitising is seeing a small amount, up to about 3, without counting. One-to-one correspondence is pairing each item with one item in the other group, so the leftovers show which has more. Counting gives each group a number, and the number that comes later when you count is more. Equal means the same number, even if the things look different.

Common mistakes: judging by the length of a row, so a spread-out row seems to have more (Piaget found that many four year olds do this); judging by the size of the things rather than how many; and mixing up more and fewer. Fewer is the right word for things you can count, and less is for amounts like water. Be careful to use both, and to ask how they know.

In the lab your child says which plate has more at a glance, then drags each car to a partner and sees that the squashed-up row has one left over. They count big balls and tiny beads, add or take away cookies to make two plates the same, and pick the plate with fewer.

familyTip: At snack time, give two people a few pieces each and ask: who has more? How do you know? Line them up in pairs to check. Then spread one pile out and ask again: has it changed?

visual.caption: Who has more? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: look and say who has more, match cars one to one, count big and tiny things, make two plates the same and find fewer.

practice.prompt: Mia has 2 grapes. Leo has 5 grapes. Who has more?
practice.hint: Match each grape of Mia's with one of Leo's. Who has some left over?
practice.explain: Leo has 5 and Mia has 2. Leo has 3 left over when you match them, so Leo has more.

practice.prompt: Mia has {a} cookies. Leo has {=a+2}. How many more cookies does Mia need to have the same as Leo?
practice.hint: Match them up in pairs. How many of Leo's cookies have no partner?
practice.explain: Leo has {=a+2} and Mia has {a}. Two of Leo's cookies have no partner, so Mia needs 2 more.

practice.prompt: 4 cars are spread out in a long row. 4 cars are squashed up close. Which row has more cars?
practice.hint: Match each car in one row with a car in the other row.
practice.explain: Both rows have 4 cars. Spreading them out makes the row longer, but it does not add any cars.

practice.prompt: Mia has {n} socks. Leo has {=n+1} socks. Who has fewer?
practice.hint: Fewer means not as many. Which number comes first when you count?
practice.explain: Mia has {n} and Leo has {=n+1}. {n} comes before {=n+1} when you count, so Mia has fewer.

pool.prompt: 3 big apples or 5 small grapes. Which group has more?
pool.hint: Count the things. Do not look at how big they are.
pool.explain: 5 is more than 3. The apples are bigger, but there are fewer of them.

pool.prompt: You match up two groups of toys. Every toy has a partner and none are left over. What do you know?
pool.hint: A toy left over would mean one group has more.
pool.explain: If every toy has a partner and nothing is left over, the two groups have the same number.

pool.prompt: Mia has {n} blocks. Leo has {=n+2} blocks. Who has more?
pool.hint: Count both groups. Which number comes later?
pool.explain: Leo has {=n+2} and Mia has {n}. {=n+2} comes later when you count, so Leo has more.

pool.prompt: Leo's 5 cars are squashed up. Mia's 5 cars are in a long row. What happens if Leo spreads his out?
pool.hint: Did he add or take away any cars?
pool.explain: Moving cars does not change how many there are. He still has 5, the same as Mia.

pool.prompt: Mia has {a} cookies. Leo has 2. How many must Mia give away to have the same as Leo?
pool.hint: Match Mia's cookies with Leo's. Count the ones with no partner.
pool.explain: Mia has {a} and Leo has 2, so {=a-2} of Mia's cookies have no partner. She gives {=a-2} away.

pool.prompt: Which word fits? Mia has 2 sweets and Leo has 4. Mia has ____ than Leo.
pool.hint: Is 2 as many as 4? Fewer means not as many.
pool.explain: 2 is not as many as 4, so Mia has fewer sweets than Leo.

pool.prompt: One plate has 1 grape. The other has 3. Which plate has more?
pool.hint: You can see 1 and 3 at a glance without counting.
pool.explain: 3 is more than 1, so the plate with 3 grapes has more.

pool.prompt: Leo has {b} ducks. Mia has 1 duck. How many more ducks does Leo have than Mia?
pool.hint: Pair Mia's duck with one of Leo's. Count Leo's ducks that are left over.
pool.explain: Leo has {b} and Mia has 1. After pairing, {=b-1} of Leo's ducks are left over, so Leo has {=b-1} more.
